claims.claim: The strategy roadmap commits that deletion of ApplicationSet-generated Applications is explicitly out of scope — 'teardown remains a manual operator action, performed one Application at a time' — while the PRD's stated goal is to ship an automated ordered deletionOrder (AllAtOnce/Reverse) for exactly those generated applications. Both cannot hold; the incident-review note already flagged the disagreement as needing an owner and none is named anywhere in the corpus.

The appset incident review adopted a standing operational rule — switch any ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting a child app, because the reverse deletion order reproduced the delete/recreate loop in T-28511 — while note-1 simultaneously reassigns the dev pair to the 'progressive sync deletion loop' whose PRD deliverable is the Reverse deletionOrder strategy. The team is scheduled to build and presumably dogfood the very configuration the interim restriction forbids operating, until the T-28511 controller fix lands; nothing sequences the fix ahead of the PRD work.

The incident review's interim rule that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists (each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave) is already violated by the pilot itself: T-27949 states the same repository is 'piloting the source hydrator' on a RollingSync ApplicationSet, with every hydration commit picked up as a source change. The restriction was written onto exactly the workstream that is running the forbidden combination, and the pilot ticket does not yet carry it.

The same hydrator-plus-progressive-sync restriction from the incident review also collides with the open request T-24578, which asks for Source Hydrator support in ApplicationSets specifically to get ordered Application create/destroy across clusters. That request combines the two features the interim rule forbids running together; granting it before the debounce exists would extend the wave-restart failure from one pilot repo to a first-class feature, and the request shows no awareness of the restriction.

The CI diff failure in T-26271 and the platform-sync decision in note-1 describe the same underlying mechanism without the ticket knowing it: with sync impersonation enabled, the diff's server-side apply dry-run runs as the destination service account, which lacks the RBAC being granted (e.g. cert-manager ClusterRole verbs). The reporter is chasing the broad cluster Secret credential while the call already root-caused it to impersonation; the root cause was agreed to be noted on the ticket but is not there.

Note-1's decision that no project flips the per-project impersonation flag 'until the diff story is fixed' blocks two other planned workstreams that depend on impersonation, and neither shows awareness: T-27833's proposed fix for the namespace privilege-escape is explicitly built on the RFC-001 service account impersonation feature, and T-28695 shows the diff story is still unfixed (Server-Side Diff ignores destinationServiceAccounts on external clusters) while also warning that the separate plan to make SSD the default (#24134) would ship the broken combination to every external-cluster user. The freeze's owner and lift condition are unnamed.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode delegates promotion to 'some external system' moving changes from the hydrateTo branch to the syncSource branch, and T-26443 documents a live failure exactly when that promoter lags (auto-sync deploys stale manifests left on the stage branch). Note-1 records that this external system is still an unowned shell script and parks the topic. A promotion-critical dependency in the hydrator design has no owner while the design and a pilot proceed on top of it.

T-28927 scopes the promotion of Progressive Sync to Stable — 'tested and validated, considered mature' — but the date is not real given open items elsewhere in the corpus: T-28511's delete/recreate loop is mitigated only by a manual runbook rule, and T-27949 shows RollingSync silently reporting a rollout complete while children are OutOfSync. Neither ticket is referenced in the promotion issue's scope, so Stable could be declared with both defects standing.

RFC-002 resolved external Helm values by rejecting multi-source in favor of the umbrella-chart (Helm dependencies) approach, but T-24417 reports that exactly this — switching to helm dependencies — 'makes it difficult to use with ApplicationSets to control the chart version across environments,' and asks for a Chart field on DrySource instead. The RFC's accepted trade-off is the blocking cost in the open request, and neither document acknowledges the other's decision.

Note-1 deprioritizes T-27327 (hydrator History & Rollback) to next quarter, but T-27327 states rollback is 'one of the first questions' in the ongoing gradual gitops-promoter + source hydrator rollout, and its design (rollback commits directly to the sync branch, bypassing the staging branch) is the only stated answer for pilots running RFC-002's push-to-stage mode. The rollout continues onboarding users onto a system whose rollback path is now scheduled a quarter behind them, and the deprioritization decision was made without the rollout owner named.
